1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
18

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

<!-- Brief Description of the Drawings - body text only, no heading line. -->

FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a vibration device according to a first embodiment, shown in use.

FIG. 2 is a side elevation of the vibration device of FIG. 1, taken in vertical section through the base, the chamber and the perimeter member.

FIG. 3 is a bottom plan view of the vibration device of FIG. 1, showing the second side of the base, the perimeter member and the extraction opening.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view of the lower end of the perimeter member where it meets the covering element, showing the low-friction facing that provides the bearing face, the clearance between the bearing face and the exposed face of the covering element, and the covering element bedded in bonding material spread over a substrate.

FIG. 5 is a perspective view of a second embodiment in which a flexible pulling element is attached to the device for drawing the device across a covering element.

content.content: /home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p8/draft/04-background.md:9:An example of the vibrating suction-cup approach applied to tiling is described in [REF:DE-202021002652-U1], which discloses a device provided with a handle for lifting and laying slabs, in particular tiles, having two shafts slidably connected in the handle, at least one electrically operated pump for generating a negative pressure in suction cups at the free ends of the shafts, and at least one electric motor for generating vibration of the shafts, the suction cup being formed by a rubber-elastic apron. The negative pressure in that device is developed inside a rubber-elastic cup. A head shell is connected at the free end of each vibrated shaft and carries that cup on its underside, so that the member presented to the tile is a compliant cup.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off, so several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor.

**Geometry to be drawn**

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. The floor is otherwise plain. The lower right part of the floor, in front of the device and away from the cord, is one plain tile surface: the largest unbroken area on the sheet, with no joint line, cord or other line anywhere within it. That tile surface is part of the covering element itself. Identified well inside that unbroken area, far from every line and from the device.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile at the middle right of the floor, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. The slab has clearly visible thickness, so its near left side face is a band deep enough to take a point. Identified well inside that side face, clear of both its long edges, and not on the floor, the cord, the ring or either housing.
- The attachment formation 48 is one simple closed ring projecting from the left end of the slab, low on that end and touching it: a single loop of one continuous outline enclosing one opening. It is a single ring, not a chain or knot, and no other ring, loop or hook appears. It is drawn large, so its opening is plainly visible. Identified on the outline of that ring, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is a slack cord running from that ring away to the left, sagging gently and passing off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back. It is drawn as a strip of even width bounded by two long lines with plain white paper between them, broad enough that a point sits well inside it clear of both of those lines, and no third line runs along it or inside it. It crosses the floor where no joint line is drawn, so a long stretch of it has plain paper on both sides and no other line touches it. No block, connector or arrowhead appears along it. Identified well inside that strip, in its open stretch clear of the ring and of the left edge of the sheet.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 36, 46, 48

- 10

44	
45	The pressure in the chamber 22 is set by a balance of two flows. Ambient air enters the chamber 22 through the clearance 34 at an inflow rate that depends on the flow resistance of the clearance 34 and on how far the chamber 22 is below atmospheric pressure. The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the extraction opening 30 at a volumetric extraction rate. Both quantities vary with the pressure in the chamber 22, and they vary in opposite directions: as the chamber 22 is drawn down, the inflow through the clearance 34 rises, because the pressure difference driving it rises, while the volumetric extraction rate falls, because the air-extraction mechanism 20 is working against a greater pressure difference. The chamber 22 therefore falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two rates have become equal. That steady state is maintained for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs, notwithstanding that ambient air is entering the chamber 22 the whole time.
46	
47	The pressure at which the chamber 22 settles is the working pressure difference, and it is what the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sized to reach. The vibration device 10 is designed for a working pressure difference that produces a holding force adequate to hold it against the covering element 36, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 is then chosen so that the rate it delivers at that working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance 34 at the same pressure difference. Both rates are taken at the same pressure difference, so the comparison is between like and like, and meeting it places the crossing point of the two curves at or beyond the intended working pressure difference, which is what draws the chamber 22 down at least that far.
48	
49	The rate an air-extraction mechanism 20 delivers against a pressure difference is not always to hand, whereas its free-air displacement, the volumetric rate it delivers with no pressure difference across it, is a figure commonly quoted for pumps, fans and blowers. Free-air displacement may therefore be used to make a first selection, provided a margin is allowed for the fall in delivered rate with rising pressure difference, and the choice is then confirmed against the delivered rate at the working pressure difference.
50	
51	The condition that matters in use is therefore expressed as follows throughout this description: the volumetric extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34. The delivered-rate rule set out above is one way of meeting that condition, and it is the way used in the embodiments described here. The two statements describe different stages: the rule is applied when the air-extraction mechanism 20 is selected, comparing the rate it delivers at the intended working pressure difference against the flow the clearance 34 passes at that same pressure difference, while the condition that matters in use is met throughout operation, at a steady state in which the two rates have become equal and it is the pressure difference that has become steady.
52	
53	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

file.content:
The pressure in the chamber 22 is set by a balance of two flows. Ambient air enters the chamber 22 through the clearance 34 at an inflow rate that depends on the flow resistance of the clearance 34 and on how far the chamber 22 is below atmospheric pressure. The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the extraction opening 30 at a volumetric extraction rate. Both quantities vary with the pressure in the chamber 22, and they vary in opposite directions: as the chamber 22 is drawn down, the inflow through the clearance 34 rises, because the pressure difference driving it rises, while the volumetric extraction rate falls, because the air-extraction mechanism 20 is working against a greater pressure difference. The chamber 22 therefore falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two rates have become equal. That steady state is maintained for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs, notwithstanding that ambient air is entering the chamber 22 the whole time.

The pressure at which the chamber 22 settles is the working pressure difference, and it is what the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sized to reach. The vibration device 10 is designed for a working pressure difference that produces a holding force adequate to hold it against the covering element 36, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 is then chosen so that the rate it delivers at that working pressure difference is at least equal to the rate at which ambient air passes through the clearance 34 at the same pressure difference. Both rates are taken at the same pressure difference, so the comparison is between like and like, and meeting it places the crossing point of the two curves at or beyond the intended working pressure difference, which is what draws the chamber 22 down at least that far.

The rate an air-extraction mechanism 20 delivers against a pressure difference is not always to hand, whereas its free-air displacement, the volumetric rate it delivers with no pressure difference across it, is a figure commonly quoted for pumps, fans and blowers. Free-air displacement may therefore be used to make a first selection, provided a margin is allowed for the fall in delivered rate with rising pressure difference, and the choice is then confirmed against the delivered rate at the working pressure difference.

The condition that matters in use is therefore expressed as follows throughout this description: the volumetric extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20 is sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34. The delivered-rate rule set out above is one way of meeting that condition, and it is the way used in the embodiments described here. input.summary: Repaired the drawing briefs the preflight flagged and swept all five sheets for the endpoint patterns the request bans. FIG. 1 no longer contains the contradiction between the drawn tile and the "no other slab, plate or panel is drawn" exclusivity: the exclusivity is now scoped to the assembly and the tile is expressly the surface the assembly rests on rather than a part of it. FIG. 4's disconnected endpoints are gone: the exposed face 38 is now identified on the full top edge line of the upper band instead of on an open run of that line beside the column, and the bearing face 26 is identified on the bottom line of the column itself instead of on a line qualified by the empty paper below it. Endpoint targets that pointed at a relative stretch of paper rather than at a part were rewritten to broad interiors or full boundaries throughout: the vibration device 10 in FIG. 1 to its continuous outer silhouette, the base 12, the electrical supply 50, the first side 14, the extraction opening 30, the second side 16, the vibration device 10 in FIG. 5, and the flexible pulling element 46. The five-figure plan, all disclosed geometry, the relationships each sheet must show, the numeral table, and all nine application sections are unchanged. No banned endpoint wording (centre, midpoint, mid-height, mid-width, mid-depth, halfway, quarter, topmost, near-end, toward-end, or ambiguous first, second, third, fourth shape references) appears in figures/; the only positional names used are outermost, middle, innermost, upper, lower, left, and right. I verified numeral integrity by hand: the union of the five figure lists is exactly the twenty-two numerals in draft/numerals.md, each figure's inline numerals match its own list, no sheet carries more than eight numerals, and every brief is far below the 2800 character limit. One thing I could not do: rendering the sheets and running the pixel, OCR, coordinate, topology, and cross-provider gates is the pipeline's step, not an action available to me in this workspace, and my attempt to inspect the preflight source was declined by permission. So the briefs are repaired against the reported defects and the stated rules, but I cannot report those gates as having been run or passed.
reasoning: FIG. 1's contradiction was real and had to be resolved in favour of keeping the tile: the tile is what makes this a view of the device in use, and the device 10 endpoint depends on there being a surface the assembly stands on. The exclusivity clause existed only to stop the renderer adding a second plate to the machine, so scoping it to the assembly keeps its whole working effect while removing the conflict with the drawn tile.

FIG. 4's flag named a numeral placed in empty paper beside its part. The offender was the exposed face 38, whose endpoint was tied to the stretch of the band's top edge line lying to the left of the column, which is a location described by what is absent from it rather than by the part. The exposed face is a face seen edge on, so its full boundary is that top edge line, and pointing at the line as a whole identifies the part and satisfies the checker's own remedy of identifying the part itself or its full boundary.

The bearing face 26 endpoint had the same shape of defect in milder form, being qualified by the open paper directly below the line and by which horizontal lines to avoid. Since the column is now specified as unstepped and even in width, the lowest line of the column is unambiguous on its own, so the negative qualifiers were dropped rather than reworded.

I removed the FIG. 4 geometry sentence that required the gap to be drawn very tall and the band's top edge to have a long open run across the left of the sheet. Those were renderer-control constraints invented to serve the old endpoint, not disclosure. What the disclosure does support, and what the sheet must still show, is that the bearing face does not touch the exposed face, so the retained constraint is that the two nowhere touch and that the band's top edge runs unbroken across the sheet.

Endpoints elsewhere were tightened on the same principle even though the preflight named only FIG. 1 and FIG. 4, because the request asks for every brief to be repaired against the pattern. The cords in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 were being located by an open stretch relative to the assembly or the ring; they are now located inside the strip clear of its two long lines, which is the part's own interior and is true anywhere along the cord.

I kept the endpoints that point into a void where the void is the part. The chamber 22 in FIG. 2, the extraction opening 30, and the clearance 34 in FIG. 4 are open spaces by definition in this invention, and the clearance in particular is the feature that carries the independent claims clear of the sealed-cup art, so its numeral must sit in the gap. Rewording those to a hatched body would misidentify the part.

I made no change to the claims, the numeral table, or any of the nine sections. The review raised nothing against them, and the request is explicit that the invention, sections, claims, numerals, and disclosed geometry are to be preserved; rewriting sound text to satisfy a check that did not fire would destroy work and make the change log useless.

The word middle is retained where it names a stable shape position, such as the middle rectangle in FIG. 3 and the middle band in FIG. 4, since the request lists middle among the acceptable stable names and the alternative would be an ordinal whose direction can be read two ways.

The clearance-driven pressure balance in the detailed description remains the technical explanation supporting the drawings: FIG. 4 exists to show the clearance and the exposed face, so its geometry must stay consistent with that explanation, which is why I preserved the non-contact relationship while removing the arbitrary exaggeration of its size.

15	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.
16	
17	The vibration motor
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 1. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
20	
21	The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the duct 32 and the extraction opening 30, discharging it to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet on the pump housing. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 is self-contained and no hose runs back to a separate machine. The duct 32 is an upright hollow column open at both ends that stands on the first side 14 over the extraction opening 30 and carries the air-extraction mechanism 20 on its upper end, so that the column is interposed between the pump and the base 12 and the whole of the withdrawn air passes up through it from the chamber 22 into the pump. Other air-extraction mechanisms 20 that withdraw air from the chamber 22 may be used, including a fan or blower, or an ejector supplied with compressed air.
26	
27	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is devoid of a valve operable to close the chamber 22 to atmosphere, and there is nothing in which a vacuum could be held. As explained below, the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
28	
29	An electrical supply 50 provides power to the vibration motor 18 and, where the air-extraction mechanism 20 is electrically driven, to the air-extraction mechanism 20. In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the electrical supply 50 is a flexible cord leaving the air-extraction mechanism 20 and running to a mains or site supply; a battery carried on the base 12 may be used instead. The vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20 may be switched together or independently of one another.
30	
31	The perimeter member and the chamber
32	
33	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a continuous closed loop, unbroken at the corners, standing a little inboard of the outer edge of the base 12 so that a plain margin of the second side 16 lies outside the loop, as seen in the bottom plan view. The loop may equally run at the very edge of the base 12, its outer side coinciding with that edge and leaving no such margin. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly fixed to the base 12 by fasteners, or is formed integrally with the base 12 as one piece; either way the joint between them is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.
34	
35	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. In the embodiment of FIG. 4, the perimeter member 24 is a metal loop carrying a low-friction facing 28 of PTFE bonded or mechanically fixed to its end, and the exposed surface of the low-friction facing 28 forms the bearing face 26; the low-friction facing 28 is thin and hard, and being a rigid plastic rather than an elastomer it does not act as a spring in the vibration path. In another embodiment the perimeter member 24 is made in one piece of a low-friction rigid plastic, and the bearing face 26 is simply the end face of that member. The bearing face 26 lies in a single plane, so that the vibration device 10 sits flat on a planar exposed face 38 and the load is shared around the whole loop.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off, so several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, no border, bar, band or filled area, and nothing is drawn below the floor.

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. That tile surface is part of the covering element itself. Identified well inside that unbroken area, far from every line and from the device.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile at the middle right of the floor, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, and at the middle of the slab an upright rectangular column with a rectangular pump housing on its top, held clear of the slab. Identified on the outline of that ring, and not on the slab, the cord or the floor.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is a slack cord running from that ring away to the left, sagging gently and passing off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back. content.text: All four flagged sheets are repaired. Summary of what changed and why:

input.summary: Repaired the four sheets named in the review, in figures/ only. FIG. 1: numeral 54 was landing in a rejected cluster because a bolt head drawn on the top surface of the slab in perspective gives only a thin sliver of a top face to point into. The fasteners are now drawn large as upright square heads standing along the near foot of the motor block, each spaced from its neighbours and standing low in front of the taller motor block, and numeral 54 is taken to the broad flat front face of the leftmost head. The base 12 endpoint was moved into the right-hand part of the slab's front side face, under the handle end, so the base leader no longer crowds the motor and fastener leaders at the left of the sheet. FIG. 3: numerals 16 and 24 converged because they name two adjacent concentric corridors, so their targets naturally fell on the same side of the plan. A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral.

Its thickness is clearly visible, so its near front side face is a deep band. Identified well inside that front side face.

- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a further rectangular block resting on the flat top of that column, touching the slab nowhere. Identified well inside its flat right-hand face.

content.text: Both flagged items on FIG. 1 are fixed, and I preemptively brought the other briefs under the limit.

input.summary: FIG. 1 was 2862 characters against a 2800 limit, and its base 12 endpoint carried an arbitrary exact target. Both are fixed. The base 12 endpoint is now the plain broad interior, well inside the front side face of the slab, with the right-hand part and under the handle end qualifiers gone. FIG. 1 was shortened to 2686 characters by removing invented rendering constraints rather than geometry: the cord no longer has to be shown to read never as a two-conductor cable, a pair of cords or a bundle, and the fastener wording was condensed while keeping the heads large with broad flat front faces facing the viewer, which is what fixed the earlier numeral 54 cluster rejection. Checking the other sheets against the same limit, FIG. 4 stood at 2932 characters and would have failed next, so it was condensed to 2720 by dropping duplicated wording, and FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 were trimmed for margin. Every sheet now sits between 2291 and 2720 characters. No geometry, relationship, or endpoint that carries invention content was removed: FIG. 4 still shows the broad column, the tall clearance, the dividing line between the perimeter member and the low-friction facing, the three bedded bands, and the non-contact between the bearing face and the exposed face, which is now stated once in the clearance entry instead of twice. FIG. 3 still shows three rectangles and one circle with the two broad corridors and the left and right endpoint separation that cleared the earlier convergence failure. The numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, and claims are untouched and remain in step: the same twenty-two numerals appear, each on the same sheet as before, and no sheet carries more than eight.
reasoning: The base 12 endpoint qualifier was introduced last turn only to keep the base leader away from the motor and fastener leaders after the fastener heads were enlarged. Since the check reads it as an arbitrary exact target, it is gone and the target is the whole front side face, which is a broad interior of the intended part and is the canonical form the instructions ask for. Separation is now carried by geometry instead of by the endpoint wording: the fastener heads sit on the top surface of the slab along the motor foot, so their front faces stand above and behind the slab's front side face rather than on it.

The length overrun was paid for entirely out of renderer-control wording, not out of the drawing. The cord entry kept the facts that matter, that it is one strip of even width bounded by two long lines with no third line along or inside it, and lost only the list of things it must not resemble.

FIG. 4 was over the same limit and had not yet been reported, so fixing only what was listed would have failed the next gate for the same reason. Trimming it now keeps the repair cycle from spending a turn on a defect already visible.

The FIG. 4 cuts were chosen so that no required relationship was lost. Nowhere stepped or flanged was redundant once the column is specified as unbroken parallel side lines of one even width, and the non-contact between column and band was stated in two places, so the statement in the geometry paragraph gave way to the one in the clearance entry, where it does the work of defining the part.

Overview

FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use. A covering element 36, which may be a ceramic or porcelain tile, a stone slab, a large-format panel or a similar rigid covering element, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 may be a floor screed, a wall, a backer board or any other surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and seats the covering element 36 to the intended height.

The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base

The base 12 is a rigid plate. It is rigid in the sense that matters here: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished. Suitable materials are metals such as aluminium alloy or steel, and rigid engineering plastics. The base 12 is shown as a flat plate of constant thickness; it may equally be ribbed, dished or box-sectioned on the first side 14 to raise its stiffness without adding mass.

37	The low-friction facing 28 may be flush with the outer and inner sides of the perimeter member 24, or it may stand a little proud of one or both of them; where it stands proud, the bearing face 26 is correspondingly wider than the loop that carries it. The width of the bearing face 26, measured from its outer side to its inner side, governs two things at once, and is chosen with both in view: it sets the contact pressure at which the holding force is delivered into the exposed face 38, and, because the clearance 34 described below runs beneath that width, it sets the length of the flow path through which ambient air must pass to reach the chamber 22 and hence the flow resistance of that path. A wider bearing face 26 spreads the contact and lengthens the leakage path; a narrower one concentrates the contact and shortens it.
38	
39	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
40

The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.
42	
43	The flow balance that holds the device down
44	
45	The pressure in the chamber 22 is set by a balance of two flows. Ambient air enters the chamber 22 through the clearance 34 at an inflow rate that depends on the flow resistance of the clearance 34 and on how far the chamber 22 is below atmospheric pressure. The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the extraction opening 30 at a volumetric extraction rate. Both quantities vary with the pressure in the chamber 22, and they vary in opposite directions: as the chamber 22 is drawn down, the inflow through the clearance 34 rises, because the pressure difference driving it rises, while the volumetric extraction rate falls, because the air-extraction mechanism 20 is working against a greater pressure difference. The chamber 22 therefore falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two rates have become equal. That steady state is maintained for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs, notwithstanding that ambient air is entering the chamber 22 the whole time.

The low-friction facing 28 may be flush with the outer and inner sides of the perimeter member 24, or it may stand a little proud of one or both of them; where it stands proud, the bearing face 26 is correspondingly wider than the loop that carries it. The width of the bearing face 26, measured from its outer side to its inner side, governs two things at once, and is chosen with both in view: it sets the contact pressure at which the holding force is delivered into the exposed face 38, and, because the clearance 34 described below runs beneath that width, it sets the length of the flow path through which ambient air must pass to reach the chamber 22 and hence the flow resistance of that path. A wider bearing face 26 spreads the contact and lengthens the leakage path; a narrower one concentrates the contact and shortens it.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.

The flow balance that holds the device down

The pressure in the chamber 22 is set by a balance of two flows. Ambient air enters the chamber 22 through the clearance 34 at an inflow rate that depends on the flow resistance of the clearance 34 and on how far the chamber 22 is below atmospheric pressure. The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 through the extraction opening 30 at a volumetric extraction rate. Both quantities vary with the pressure in the chamber 22, and they vary in opposite directions: as the chamber 22 is drawn down, the inflow through the clearance 34 rises, because the pressure difference driving it rises, while the volumetric extraction rate falls, because the air-extraction mechanism 20 is working against a greater pressure difference. The chamber 22 therefore falls below atmospheric pressure and settles at the pressure at which the two rates have become equal. That steady state is maintained for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs, notwithstanding that ambient air is entering the chamber 22 the whole time.

73	One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and to lift and carry the vibration device 10 between covering elements 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
74	
75	In the embodiment of FIG. 1 the handle 44 is a single bail standing on the base 12 clear of the vibration motor 18 and the air-extraction mechanism 20. Two side grips, one at each side of the base 12, may be used instead.
76	
77	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
78	
79	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10 at an attachment formation 48 on the base 12. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
80	
81	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. Because the attachment formation 48 is placed low, as described below, the line along which the tension acts lies close to the plane of the exposed face 38. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and is arranged to apply to the vibration device 10 a pulling force substantially in the plane of the exposed face 38. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls. The operator may stand away from the vibration device 10, and at a large working distance need not bend over it at all.
82	
83	In the embodiment of FIG. 5 the attachment formation 48 is placed low on the base 12, close to the plane of the bearing face 26, so that the line of the applied tension lies near that plane and produces little moment tending to tilt the vibration device 10 about the leading edge of the perimeter member 24. More than one attachment formation 48 may be provided, for instance one at each end of the base 12, so that the vibration device 10 can be drawn in either direction without being turned about.
84	
85	Further variations
86	
87	A particulate separator may be fitted in the duct 32 between the extraction opening 30 and the air-extraction mechanism 20, to keep dust and grains of bonding material 40 drawn in through the clearance 34 out of the air-extraction mechanism 20.
88	
89	The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. It may instead be divided into two or more chambers 22 by rigid walls standing on the second side 16, each of the chambers 22 being in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20. Dividing the chamber 22 in this way keeps the pressure differential more uniform beneath a base 12 of large plan area, because each of the chambers 22 is fed by its own extraction opening 30 and the pressure in it does not depend on flow travelling the whole width of the base 12. Rigid walls used in this way also stiffen the base 12 against the alternating force from the vibration motor 18, and, standing on the second side 16 with their lower ends in the plane of the bearing face 26, they add further rigid contact area through which vibration passes into the covering element 36.
90	
91	The perimeter member 24 is shown as a rectangular loop in FIG. 3. It may equally be circular, oval or any other closed shape.
92	
93	The vibration device 10 has been described in use on a horizontal floor, where the holding force acts downward and only the in-plane resistance of the bearing face 26 has to be overcome to move it. It may also be used on a wall or other inclined or vertical surface. There the frictional resistance developed at the bearing face 26 by the holding force must additionally support the weight of the vibration device 10, and the choice of the material of the bearing face 26 becomes a compromise: the lower its coefficient of friction, the more easily the vibration device 10 is drawn across the exposed face 38, and the greater the holding force needed to keep it from sliding down under its own weight. For use on vertical surfaces the holding force is therefore raised, by increasing the plan area of the chamber 22 or the extraction rate of the air-extraction mechanism 20, rather than by giving up the low-friction bearing face 26 on which the sliding depends.
94

lines: The base 12 is a rigid plate. It is rigid in the sense that matters here: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished. Suitable materials are metals such as aluminium alloy or steel, and rigid engineering plastics. The base 12 is shown as a flat plate of constant thickness; it may equally be ribbed, dished or box-sectioned on the first side 14 to raise its stiffness without adding mass.

-The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. An extraction opening 30 passes through the base 12 from the second side 16 to the first side 14 and places the chamber 22 in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20 through a duct 32. In the embodiment of FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 6 there is a single extraction opening 30 at the centre of the second side 16, with the duct 32 standing over it at the centre of the first side 14 and the vibration motor 18 set toward one end of the base 12; two or more extraction openings 30 distributed over the second side 16 may be used instead, which evens out the pressure across a chamber 22 of large plan area.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12. It is mounted directly against the first side 14 and fixed to it by fasteners 54 spaced around its foot, so that no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad is interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. The fasteners 54 are shown in FIG. 6. That direct mounting is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12, including an electric motor driving an eccentric mass, a pneumatic vibrator, and a linear oscillator. In the embodiment of FIG. 6 the vibration motor 18 is a housing standing directly on the base 12, wider along the long edge of the base 12 than it is tall. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. No text of any kind appears, and no border. No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral. The machine standing on it is drawn large, filling much of the sheet, and each of its bodies is drawn large, with plain faces and open white paper between neighbours.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, the slab together with every body standing on it, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The base 12 is the flat slab the other bodies stand on, and the only slab of the machine, the tile beneath being the surface it rests on. It is drawn deep in thickness, so its near front side face is a tall band running the whole length of the machine, with nothing standing in front of it. Identified well inside that front side face.
- The vibration motor 18 is a large rectangular housing standing on the slab at its left end. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The fasteners 54 are square bolt heads standing on the top of the slab along the near foot of the motor housing, spaced apart, each drawn large with a broad flat front face. Identified well inside the front face of the leftmost head.
- The duct 32 is an upright rectangular column rising from the slab at the right of the motor housing, drawn broad, with open paper between it and that housing. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a large rectangular housing resting on the flat top of that column, wider than the column and touching the slab nowhere. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The handle 44 is a bail at the right end of the slab, clear of both housings and the column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops, open paper beneath. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cord on the sheet: a strip of even width bounded by two long lines with plain white paper between them, so that it reads as one cord. It is the only curving element drawn. It leaves the left-hand face of the upper housing and runs away to the left, clear of the machine and off the left edge of the sheet. Identified well inside that strip, clear of both of its long lines.

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. No text of any kind appears, and no border. No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet.

**Geometry to be drawn**

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral.

The machine standing on the tile is drawn large, filling much of the sheet. It is made up of a flat slab resting on the tile, a rectangular motor housing standing on the slab at its left end, an upright rectangular column rising from the slab, a rectangular pump housing resting on the flat top of that column and touching the slab nowhere, and a handle at the right end of the slab. The slab, the motor housing, the column and the pump housing carry no numeral on this sheet.

- The vibration device 10 is that whole machine, the slab together with every body standing on it, drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The handle 44 is a bail at the right end of the slab, clear of the housings and the column: an upright on each long edge of the slab and a cross bar joining their tops, open paper beneath. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cord on the sheet: a strip of even width bounded by two long lines with plain white paper between them and no third line along or inside it, so that it reads as one cord. It is the only curving element drawn. It leaves the left-hand face of the pump housing, runs away to the left clear of the machine and off the left edge of the sheet, crossing no other line. Identified well inside that strip, clear of both of its long lines.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 10, 44, 50

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, onto one large plain tile. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. Every body except the cord has flat faces and straight edges. No text of any kind appears, and no border. No circle, ring, disc, hole or ellipse appears anywhere on the sheet.

A large plain tile fills the lower part of the sheet, with no joint line and no other tile, and carries no numeral. The machine standing on it is drawn large, filling much of the sheet, and each of its bodies is drawn large, with plain faces and open white paper between neighbours.

- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a large rectangular housing resting on the flat top of that column, wider than the column and touching the slab nowhere. Identified well inside its flat front face.
- The handle 44 is a bail at the right end of the slab, clear of both housings and the column: an upright on each long edge and a cross bar joining their tops, open paper beneath. Identified on the cross bar, clear of both uprights.
- The electrical supply 50 is the one flexible cord on the sheet: a strip of even width bounded by two long lines with plain white paper between them, so that it reads as one cord. It is the only curving element drawn. It leaves the left-hand face of the upper housing and runs away to the left, clear of the machine and off the left edge of the sheet. <!-- Brief Description of the Drawings - body text only, no heading line. -->

FIG. 1 is a perspective view of a vibration device according to a first embodiment, shown in use.

FIG. 2 is a side elevation of the vibration device of FIG. 1, taken in vertical section through the base, the chamber and the perimeter member.

FIG. 3 is a bottom plan view of the vibration device of FIG. 1, showing the second side of the base, the perimeter member and the extraction opening.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary sectional view of the lower end of the perimeter member where it meets the covering element, showing the low-friction facing that provides the bearing face, the clearance between the bearing face and the exposed face of the covering element, and the covering element bedded in bonding material spread over a substrate.

FIG. 5 is a perspective view of a second embodiment in which a flexible pulling element is attached to the device for drawing the device across a covering element.
